strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical guarantee (Proposition 4.1, with full proof in Appendix A.1) that the proposed mixing policy exactly recovers the target distribution under linear scalarization, which is a genuine advance over prior training-free composition schemes for GFlowNets that lack such guarantees.

Unifies two previously disjoint lines of work (scalarization and logical/compositional operators) under a single training-free mixing framework, whereas prior methods (MOGFN, HN-GFN, compositional sculpting) each handle only one paradigm and require retraining or an auxiliary classifier.

The distortion-factor analysis (Section 4.2, Eq. 6, Eq. 9) gives an interpretable decomposition of the approximation error for non-linear operators, and the empirical study (Fig. 3, Fig. A6) convincingly shows that deviations concentrate in low-density regions that matter least for sampling.

Experiments span both a controlled synthetic 2D-grid domain (where ground-truth distributions are computable, enabling exact L1 evaluation) and two realistic molecule-generation settings (fragment-based and atom-based/QM9), lending some breadth to the empirical validation.

The method is dramatically more efficient than the classifier-guided baseline for logical operators (40-70x faster inference, Table 5) and, notably, better preserves molecule validity than classifier guidance (Table 6), which degrades sharply with more composed objectives (54.8% valid with 3 objectives vs 99.8% for the proposed method).

A simple ensemble ablation (mixing policies without reaching-probability weighting) is included and shown to perform substantially worse, supporting the paper's central claim that the flow-based weighting u_i(s) is the key mechanistic ingredient.
Reasonably thorough reproducibility details (architectures, optimizers, hyperparameters) are provided in the appendix for both synthetic and real-world experiments.
weaknesses: The exactness guarantee and the practical reaching-probability estimator (u_i(s) = F_i(s)/Z_i) require GFlowNet training objectives that explicitly parameterize state flow (FM, DB, SubTB); models trained with Trajectory Balance, which is one of the most commonly used objectives in practice, are explicitly stated to be incompatible, limiting the method's general applicability.

On real-world molecule generation, the scalarization results (Table 3) are mixed rather than clearly favorable: HN-GFN outperforms the proposed method on several fragment-based reward pairs (SEH-SA, SA-QED) in both reward and diversity, and diversity is often lower for the proposed method across both fragment- and atom-based tasks, weakening the claim of matching or exceeding baseline performance.

The theoretical analysis for non-linear composition (β≠1 scalarization and logical operators) does not provide a formal, quantitative bound on the total variation distance or L1 error despite the abstract's claim to "quantify the approximation quality... through a distortion factor"; the actual treatment is empirical/qualitative (observing δ(x) is approximately constant in high-density regions) rather than a derived analytic bound.

The method incurs non-trivial inference overhead relative to conditioned models for scalarization (Table 5, roughly 1.5-3x slower per sample, worse on QM9), since it must query all k base models at every generation step; this cost grows with the number of objectives and is not parallelized in the current implementation, though the paper does not explore whether such overhead would compound problematically at larger k or with larger base models.

The contrast (subtraction) operator is shown in the appendix (Table A6, Fig. A7) to fail when objectives are positively correlated in the generated samples, but this important failure mode is relegated to the appendix rather than discussed as a core limitation in the main text.

All theoretical results assume the pre-trained GFlowNets have converged to their exact target distributions (p_i ≈ p*_i); there is no analysis of how imperfect base-model training (a realistic scenario) propagates through the mixing rule and affects the exactness/approximation guarantees.

The core algorithmic idea—reweighting/mixing per-step policies by a state-relevance/flow quantity—is conceptually related to existing model-composition techniques (products of experts, classifier-free/guidance-based composition in diffusion models); while its specific instantiation for GFlowNet forward policies via reaching probabilities is new, the degree of conceptual novelty beyond adapting known composition principles to a new generative model class is moderate.

strengths: The paper provides a clean, provable theoretical result (Proposition 4.1) showing that the proposed reaching-probability-weighted mixing policy exactly recovers the target distribution for linear scalarization, which is a genuinely novel guarantee not previously established for training-free GFlowNet composition.
The framework unifies two previously separate lines of work (scalarization and logical/compositional operators) under a single mixing rule, which is conceptually elegant.

The synthetic 2D grid experiments are well-controlled, allow exact ground-truth computation, and clearly demonstrate that the proposed reaching-probability weighting is essential (the naive 'ensemble' ablation performs much worse), supporting the core mechanistic claim.

On real molecular generation benchmarks, the method is shown to preserve molecule validity much better than the classifier-guided baseline and is 40-70x faster at inference for logical composition, which is a practically meaningful advantage.
The paper is generally clearly written, with a thorough appendix including derivations and extensive additional results/ablations (e.g., distortion factor analysis, reward correlation discussion).
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'quantifying approximation quality through a distortion factor' for non-linear/logical operators is weaker than advertised: no formal bound on the total variation distance is actually derived (despite the introduction claiming such an analysis); Section 4.2 and Eq. (9) merely restate the L1 error in terms of δ(x) and show empirically that δ(x) is close to constant in high-density regions, which is an observation rather than a theoretical guarantee.

The method's reliance on explicitly learned state flow F(s) restricts its applicability to GFlowNet objectives that parameterize state flow (FM, DB, SubTB) and explicitly excludes Trajectory Balance (TB)-trained models, which are arguably the most common and stable choice for larger/more complex state spaces in practice; this significant practical limitation is only briefly acknowledged in the appendix rather than discussed as a core limitation in the main text.

On the real-world molecular generation scalarization task (Table 3), the proposed training-free method does not consistently outperform the trained baselines (HN-GFN wins on several reward metrics and both baselines often win on diversity), so the claim that the method 'matches or exceeds' trained baselines is only partially supported and somewhat overstated.

Experimental scale is modest relative to the paper's motivating claims about 'real-world scientific discovery': the fragment-based vocabulary (72 fragments, ≤9 fragments/molecule) and QM9 atom-based tasks are comparatively small state spaces, leaving open how well the approach scales to larger, more realistic generative settings (e.g., larger molecules, proteins).

There is no analysis of how approximation/estimation error in the learned flow F_i(s) and partition function Z_i (as opposed to the idealized exact quantities used in the theoretical proof) propagates into the exactness guarantee in practice; Proposition 4.1 is proved under an idealized setting that may not hold with imperfect pretrained models.

The 'ensemble' baseline used to justify the importance of reaching-probability weighting is a fairly weak strawman (simple averaging without any weighting), and no stronger alternative heuristic weighting scheme is compared against, which limits how convincingly the specific choice of u_i(s) as the weight is justified over other plausible weighting functions.

No statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or confidence intervals are reported for the main quantitative results (Tables 1-5), making it difficult to assess the robustness of the reported differences, especially where margins are small (e.g., Table 2, Table 4).

strengths: Unifies two previously separate paradigms (scalarization and logical composition of multi-objective GFlowNets) into a single training-free mixing framework, which is a genuine conceptual contribution not previously addressed jointly.

Provides a rigorous theoretical result (Proposition 4.1, with full proof in Appendix A.1 via explicit construction and induction showing the mixed forward policy induces the exact reaching-probability recursion) establishing exact recovery of the target distribution for linear scalarization -- a non-trivial guarantee that prior training-free composition approaches for GFlowNets lack.

Introduces a principled distortion-factor analysis (δ(x)) for non-linear operators, decomposing the L1 approximation error analytically (Appendix A.3) and empirically showing the distortion is near-constant in high-density/high-reward regions, which is exactly where sample quality matters most.

Extensive empirical validation across a controlled synthetic 2D grid (where ground truth is tractable) and two realistic molecular generation benchmarks (fragment-based and atom-based QM9), covering both scalarization (2-5 objectives) and logical operators (harmonic mean, contrast, chained to 3 objectives).

Strong practical advantages demonstrated: 40-70x faster inference than classifier-guided compositional sculpting, no need to train auxiliary classifiers, graceful degradation (near-constant error) as the number of objectives increases unlike MOGFN/HN-GFN, and notably better validity of generated molecules compared to classifier guidance (which drops to ~55% validity with 3 objectives).
Good ablation design: the 'ensemble' baseline without reaching-probability weighting clearly isolates and justifies the key technical idea (flow-based weighting) driving the gains.
Reasonably transparent and reproducible methodology, with detailed hyperparameters, architectures, and training procedures provided in the appendix for both synthetic and real-world experiments.
weaknesses: The practical applicability of the reaching-probability estimator is restricted to GFlowNet training objectives that explicitly parameterize state flow (FM, DB, SubTB); it is incompatible with Trajectory Balance (TB), which is widely considered one of the most effective and commonly used GFlowNet objectives in practice, somewhat limiting the 'plug-and-play with any pre-trained GFlowNet' claim.

For non-linear composition (general logical operators, and scalarization with β≠1, which is used in essentially all the real molecule experiments), there is no formal error bound -- only an empirical observation on a small set of examples that distortion is low in high-density regions. The theoretical story is therefore considerably weaker than the paper's framing suggests, and the single exactness proof covers a comparatively narrow case (β=1 linear scalarization) while essentially all reported real-world scalarization experiments rely on an additional ad hoc 'reward-sharpened mixing' trick (Appendix B.2.1) without formal guarantees.

Results for logical operators are only 'comparable' to classifier guidance rather than consistently better (Tables 2 and 4 show mixed wins/losses on the grid, and inconsistent gains on molecules for some reward pairs e.g. Table A6 shows the contrast operator failing when rewards are positively correlated), suggesting the approximation quality is sensitive to reward correlation structure, a limitation acknowledged only briefly.

Scalarization results on real molecular tasks are likewise mixed (Table 3): the proposed method does not consistently dominate MOGFN/HN-GFN in reward or diversity, and the paper's own interpretation ('neither method consistently outperforms the other') somewhat undercuts the significance of the claimed advantage, leaving the main benefit as computational/training-cost savings rather than sample quality.

The requirement to have access to the internal flow function F(s) (and the correct normalizing constant Z) assumes a specific training/parameterization regime; truly 'off-the-shelf' pre-trained GFlowNets obtained via TB or without saved flow heads would not be directly usable, which is a meaningful practical caveat not strongly foregrounded in the main text.

Inference time overhead for scalarization (relative to MOGFN/HN-GFN) grows with trajectory length and number of objectives (Table 5), and the paper notes the implementation does not parallelize base-model forward passes, leaving open whether the reported efficiency gains would hold under a more optimized implementation or with many more base models.

strengths: Provides a clean, rigorously proven theoretical result (Proposition 4.1, with full derivation in Appendix A.1) showing that mixing forward policies weighted by reaching probability exactly recovers the target distribution for linear scalarization — a non-trivial and elegant contribution.

Unifies two previously separate lines of work (scalarization and logical-operator composition) under a single training-free mixing framework, addressing a genuine practical limitation of prior methods (MOGFN/HN-GFN require retraining, compositional sculpting requires a new classifier per objective set).

Offers two complementary and practical routes (Model F and DB F) for computing reaching probabilities, making the method compatible with essentially all standard GFlowNet training objectives (FM, DB, SubTB, TB), which increases applicability and reproducibility.

Strong, well-designed empirical validation: synthetic 2D-grid experiments where ground truth is exactly computable show substantially lower L1 error than preference-conditioned baselines and scale gracefully with the number of objectives; molecule-generation experiments (fragment- and atom-based) show performance matching or exceeding jointly trained baselines.

Significant and clearly demonstrated efficiency advantage over classifier-guided composition (30–65x faster inference) with quantified overhead versus preference-conditioned baselines, which is practically important for iterative scientific discovery workflows.

Careful, honest empirical analysis of the distortion factor δ(x) for nonlinear operators showing approximation is best where it matters (high-density regions) and identifying explicitly when the method struggles (e.g., positively correlated objectives degrading the contrast operator, Table A9/Fig. A8), reflecting good scientific transparency.

Extensive ablations (ensemble baseline without reaching-probability weighting, comparison across SubTB/TB training objectives, validity checks, multiple MOO metrics such as hypervolume/IGD+/Pareto count) and very detailed hyperparameter/appendix documentation supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: For nonlinear composition operators (β≠1 scalarization and logical operators), the method is only approximately correct, and the approximation quality is validated solely in the small synthetic 2D-grid domain where ground truth is tractable; no analogous fidelity check is possible or attempted for the real-world molecular tasks, leaving open how well the distortion-factor argument generalizes to larger/more complex state spaces.

Empirical results on logical operators (Table 2, Table 5) are mixed rather than uniformly favorable — the method outperforms classifier guidance on some reward pairs but underperforms on others, and the paper's narrative of 'comparable performance' understates this variability.

The method still fundamentally depends on having access to k pre-trained single-objective GFlowNets; introducing a genuinely new objective still requires training a new base model (even though this is cheaper than joint retraining), so the 'no retraining' claim mainly saves the composition/combination stage rather than eliminating training entirely.

Real-world experiments use fairly modest state-space sizes (72-fragment vocabulary, QM9 atom-based generation) and at most 3 objectives; scalability to larger combinatorial spaces, more objectives, or more complex molecular representations is not empirically demonstrated.

The contrast (subtraction) operator is shown to struggle noticeably when underlying reward objectives are positively correlated (Table A9), a meaningful practical limitation for realistic multi-property drug-design settings where objectives are rarely independent.

The core methodological idea — reweighting forward-policy transitions by reaching probability — is a relatively simple combination rule; while the theoretical exactness result for linear scalarization is valuable, the overall novelty relative to compositional sculpting and other model-composition literature is somewhat incremental in framing.

strengths: The paper offers a clean, rigorously proven theoretical result (Proposition 4.1, with full derivation in Appendix A.1) that the proposed reaching-probability-weighted mixing policy exactly recovers the target distribution under linear scalarization, which is a genuine and useful contribution.

The two practical routes for computing the reaching probability (Model F for FM/DB/SubTB-trained models, DB F for TB-trained models via the detailed balance identity) make the method broadly compatible with existing GFlowNet training objectives without requiring changes to how base models are trained.

The framework unifies two previously separate lines of work (scalarization and logical/compositional operators) under a single training-free inference-time mechanism, addressing a real practical pain point (retraining cost for every new objective combination).

Experiments span a controlled synthetic 2D grid (where ground truth is computable) and two realistic molecular generation settings (fragment-based and atom-based/QM9), providing reasonably broad empirical coverage.

For logical operators, the method is 30-65x faster at inference than the classifier-guidance baseline of compositional sculpting, which is a clear and practically meaningful advantage since classifier guidance must enumerate all successor states at every step.

The paper includes honest limitation analysis, including the distortion-factor study (Section 5.3, Fig. 3) and an explicit failure case (Table A9) where the contrast operator struggles when reward objectives are positively correlated among generated samples.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee (exact recovery) applies only to the simplest case, linear scalarization with beta=1; for the more interesting nonlinear/logical composition cases, which arguably constitute the paper's main claimed novelty over prior scalarization-only work, there is no formal error bound, only an empirical/qualitative claim that the distortion factor 'remains approximately constant' in high-density regions. Figures 3(b)-(c) and A6 actually show a considerable number of outliers and non-trivial variation even in what is described as the relevant region, weakening this claim.

Empirical superiority over baselines is frequently only 'comparable' rather than clearly better: in Table 2 (grid logical operators) results are mixed, with the classifier-guided baseline winning on several reward pairs; in Table 3/4 (molecule scalarization) gains over MOGFN/HN-GFN are often marginal and diversity is sometimes worse; in Table 5 improvements over classifier guidance, while generally positive, are modest in several rows (e.g., atom-based contrast operator).

For scalarization on molecular tasks, the proposed method is actually slower per sample (8-40 ms) than MOGFN/HN-GFN/OP-GFN (Table 6), so the practical benefit in this regime is limited to avoiding retraining rather than to sample quality or speed, and this trade-off is not deeply analyzed (e.g., no discussion of amortized cost when many new objective combinations are needed vs. cost of a single joint retraining).

The method's real-world applicability is undermined in cases where reward objectives are positively correlated in the generated sample distribution (Table A9, Fig. A8); the contrast operator fails to isolate the intended region in these cases, and this is a fairly common practical scenario (e.g., drug-likeness and synthesizability are often correlated), suggesting the approach's robustness across the space of real objective combinations is more limited than the main results imply.

The synthetic grid results (Tables 1, 2) do not report variance/uncertainty over random seeds or initializations, making it hard to assess whether the reported L1 error differences (e.g., 0.003 vs 0.017-0.048 for scalarization) are statistically robust or sensitive to a single training run of each baseline.

The reliance on the DB F route's detailed balance identity assumes the base GFlowNet has converged to satisfy detailed balance exactly; no analysis is given of how imperfect convergence of pre-trained models (a realistic scenario) propagates into errors in the recovered reaching probabilities and hence the composed distribution.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important limitation of prior multi-objective GFlowNet methods (retraining for every new combination of objectives or logical operator), and proposes a training-free, inference-time composition mechanism.

The framework is unified: it handles both linear scalarization and nonlinear logical operators (harmonic mean, contrast) within a single mixing rule, whereas prior work (MOGFN/HN-GFN vs. compositional sculpting) treats these separately.

Strong theoretical contribution: Proposition 4.1 and its detailed appendix proof rigorously establish exact recovery of the target distribution for linear scalarization, which is a non-trivial and clean result.

Honest and useful analysis of the approximation quality for nonlinear operators via the distortion factor δ(x), including empirical verification that deviations concentrate in low-density regions that matter least for sampling quality (Section 5.3, Fig. 3).

Two practical routes for computing the reaching probability (Model F and DB F) make the method compatible with essentially all standard GFlowNet training objectives (FM, DB, SubTB, TB), improving applicability.

Comprehensive experimental validation: controlled synthetic 2D grid experiments with exact ground-truth distributions, plus two realistic molecule-generation domains (fragment-based and atom-based QM9), covering both scalarization and logical operators.

Meaningful ablations, e.g., the ensemble baseline (mixing without reaching-probability weighting) clearly shows the necessity of the proposed weighting scheme, and the reward-correlation analysis (Table A9, Fig. A8) provides insight into when the contrast operator underperforms.

Substantial practical benefit demonstrated: the method is 30–65x faster at inference than classifier-guided composition, since it avoids enumerating all successor states, while maintaining or improving reward/hypervolume/validity metrics relative to baselines that require joint or auxiliary training.
weaknesses: For nonlinear composition (β≠1 scalarization and logical operators), there is no formal error bound—only an empirical/qualitative argument that distortion is small in high-density regions; a more rigorous characterization (e.g., a provable bound on L1 error in terms of properties of G) would strengthen the theoretical contribution.

Performance on logical operators is only 'comparable' to classifier guidance rather than uniformly better (Table 2, Table 5 show mixed wins/losses), and diversity in molecule generation is sometimes slightly lower than baselines (Table 3), tempering the significance of the improvement.

Scalability of the method to larger numbers of objectives is only convincingly tested on the synthetic grid (up to 5 objectives); real-world molecule experiments are limited to 2–3 objectives, leaving open how the approach scales with more pre-trained components in practice.

The DB F route relies on a multiplicative product of forward/backward policy ratios along a trajectory to reconstruct the reaching probability, which could be numerically unstable or high-variance for longer trajectories; this is not analyzed empirically (e.g., variance of the estimator, sensitivity to trajectory length).

The method's practicality hinges on the availability of high-quality pre-trained single-objective GFlowNets for every objective of interest, and the paper does not explore how sensitive the composition quality is to imperfectly trained or under-converged base models.

Total end-to-end cost (training all base models across many single objectives vs. training joint/preference-conditioned models) is not directly compared, only inference-time cost; a fuller accounting of when the training-free advantage actually pays off would be useful for practitioners.
